reviewed_input.mode: Read complete actual learner draft and independently solve all 25 tasks in writing.

key_blind.statement: No pronunciation key, old or revised, was opened for this review. The earlier source and glossary-scope work inspected primary evidence and dictionary entries, not answer keys. Solutions precede comparison.
key_blind.stage: Before independent solutions were frozen; these false values describe that preserved blind stage, not the subsequent authorized comparison.

solutions.label: A1
solutions.independent_answer: For has brief rounded short o: start near caught if available, or lower the jaw slightly from the first part of go while keeping rounded lips. Fōr has long ō: hold the steady beginning of go, without its final glide. Duration changes, and the guide’s practical short/long approximations also differ in quality.
solutions.scope: application of printed sound rules with meanings supplied

solutions.label: A2
solutions.independent_answer: Węnde has short e as in bet; its hook adds no separate sound. Wēnde has long ē: hold the beginning of day without the final glide. Both words have an audible light final e and two syllables.
solutions.scope: application of printed sound rules with meanings supplied

solutions.label: A3
solutions.independent_answer: Dǣd: hold the cat vowel. Wīd: hold the vowel of see, without the diphthong of modern wide. Hȳdan: hold the see tongue position while rounding the lips as for oo. The tongue stays forward; lip rounding distinguishes ȳ from ī. Dǣd and wīd have one syllable each; hȳdan has two.
solutions.scope: application of printed sound rules with meanings supplied

solutions.label: A4
solutions.independent_answer: Eall: short cat-to-oo movement, one syllable. Scēap: long cat-to-oo movement, one syllable. Heorte: short steady-day-to-oo movement, two syllables (heo-rte). Frēond: long steady-day-to-oo movement, one syllable. Scield: short see-to-oo movement, one syllable. Gīet: long see-to-oo movement, one syllable. In each long diphthong hold its first part longer; no diphthong receives two beats.
solutions.scope: application of printed sound rules with meanings supplied

solutions.label: B1
solutions.independent_answer: The c is ch as in chin. It is word-initial and immediately followed by the front diphthong ēo, so the initial front-vowel branch applies.
solutions.scope: application of printed sound rules with meanings supplied

solutions.label: B2
solutions.independent_answer: The sounds differ. In micel, c follows i and precedes e: use ch. In micles, c immediately precedes the consonant l: use k. Check the immediate following consonant before applying the after-i pattern.
solutions.scope: application of printed sound rules with meanings supplied

solutions.label: B3
solutions.independent_answer: Both g letters are stopped g as in go. In gān, a back vowel immediately follows g; in glæd, l immediately follows it. Neither enters the initial y-sound branch. Having selected non-y g, its word-initial position selects stopped g. The later æ across l does not change that.
solutions.scope: application of printed sound rules with meanings supplied

solutions.label: B4
solutions.independent_answer: Both g letters have y as in yes. In fæger, g follows front æ and no back vowel follows; in regn, g follows front e and is followed by n rather than a back vowel. The following n does not force stopped g. These satisfy the y branch, so the later non-y rule is not applied.
solutions.scope: application of printed sound rules with meanings supplied

solutions.label: B5
solutions.independent_answer: The g is continuous voiced back g. The surrounding ā and a are back vowels, so the y branch does not apply. The single g is medial and is neither after n nor a supplied hard doubled consonant, so it is continuous rather than stopped. Hold the back of the tongue near the hard-g position with a narrow gap; let air pass while the throat vibrates.
solutions.scope: application of printed sound rules with meanings supplied

solutions.label: B6
solutions.independent_answer: Brycg has the final consonant sound of bridge for cg. Its y is short: use the bit tongue position with rounded lips, not ordinary unrounded i. Singan has ng as in finger, including the audible stopped g; it is not the ng of singer without g. Read the combinations as units before applying single-letter rules.
solutions.scope: application of printed sound rules with meanings supplied

solutions.label: B7
solutions.independent_answer: Riht has the front, unvoiced h-like sound: the preceding i brings the tongue forward, and the middle of the tongue narrows the passage near the roof of the mouth. Dohtor has the back, unvoiced h-like sound: after o, raise the back of the tongue near the k position but leave a gap for breath. Keep t audible in both.
solutions.scope: application of printed sound rules with meanings supplied

solutions.label: B8
solutions.independent_answer: Sc in scūfan is the single sh sound of ship; ū does not turn it into s+k because the combination rule is checked first. Cw in cwæð is the sequence k+w, joined without an inserted vowel. It is not one ch sound.
solutions.scope: application of printed sound rules with meanings supplied

solutions.label: C1
solutions.independent_answer: The f is voiced, like v in van. It stands between the voiced long ǣ vowel and voiced r; both neighbours are voiced although r is not a vowel.
solutions.scope: application of printed sound rules with meanings supplied

solutions.label: C2
solutions.independent_answer: Both f letters are unvoiced, like f in fan. One begins and the other ends the word. The final v of modern five does not supply the Old English value.
solutions.scope: application of printed sound rules with meanings supplied

solutions.label: C3
solutions.independent_answer: The s is voiced, like z in zip, between the voiced diphthong ēo and the following a. The final ð is unvoiced, like th in thin, because it ends the word. The two letters therefore need different decisions.
solutions.scope: application of printed sound rules with meanings supplied

solutions.label: C4
solutions.independent_answer: Final ð is unvoiced th as in thin. The preceding f is beside that voiceless consonant, so it too is unvoiced, as in fan. It is not between two voiced sounds.
solutions.scope: application of printed sound rules with meanings supplied

solutions.label: C5
solutions.independent_answer: Final ð is unvoiced th as in thin. Replacing eth with thorn does not change the sound: either letter can represent either th value. Final position, not the choice of letter, selects this reading.
solutions.scope: application of printed sound rules with meanings supplied

solutions.label: C6
solutions.independent_answer: Use unvoiced th in hǣlðu because the word-specific reading is explicitly supplied; the voiced l and u around it do not override that information. In ǣfre, no exception is supplied: f between the voiced vowel and r is voiced v. This compares a supplied exception with the ordinary rule; it does not deduce the exception from spelling.
solutions.scope: explicit supplied-exception comparison

solutions.label: D1
solutions.independent_answer: Sittan has two syllables, with stress on the first. Keep i short as in bit. Prolong the tt closure between the vowels, then release it into the following vowel. This adds neither vowel length nor a syllable.
solutions.scope: application of printed sound rules with meanings supplied

solutions.label: D2
solutions.independent_answer: Sunne has two syllables, with stress on sun-. Hold the medial nn longer without inserting a vowel. Keep the final e audible as a light bet vowel; the doubling does not add a third syllable.
solutions.scope: application of printed sound rules with meanings supplied

solutions.label: D3
solutions.independent_answer: Ge-writ has two syllables. The supplied ge- prefix is unstressed, so stress writ. Pronounce w and r together at the start of that root syllable without an inserted vowel. There is no doubled consonant.
solutions.scope: application of printed sound rules with meanings supplied

solutions.label: D4
solutions.independent_answer: For-lǣtan has three syllables, with main stress on the second, lǣ-. The prefixed verb places stress on its root rather than for-. The macron separately says to hold the ǣ vowel longer; it does not itself assign stress. There is no doubled consonant.
learner_rule_or_support: supplied division and verb identification in D4
solutions.scope: application of printed sound rules with meanings supplied

solutions.label: E1
solutions.independent_answer: The g of supplied ge- has y as in yes before e. The sc is sh as in ship. Ge-scēop has two syllables with stress on scēop; the long ēo remains one glide within the root syllable.
solutions.scope: application of printed sound rules with meanings supplied

solutions.label: E2
solutions.independent_answer: The f is voiced v as in van: it is between the voiced eo diphthong and o. Heofonan has three syllables, heo-fo-nan; eo has one beat.
solutions.scope: application of printed sound rules with meanings supplied

solutions.label: E3
solutions.independent_answer: The ð is voiced th as in this. It lies between voiced r and the following a vowel. The ordinary rule requires voiced sounds on both sides, not two vowels, so the consonantal left neighbour is no obstacle.
solutions.scope: application of printed sound rules with meanings supplied

coverage.assessment: Marks, hooked letters, thorn/eth, long versus stressed, and diphthong syllables are clear and sufficient.

American cues are practical, with a rounded-o fallback, long front-rounded articulation and explicit stressed-syllable scope for a before nasals. The accepted traditional approximations are distinguished from exact reconstruction.
Fulk’s selected rounded convention is stated consistently; long first elements and one-beat diphthongs support A4. The geong exception is explicitly supplied.

Combination priority, different c/g conditioning, immediate neighbours, and separate palatal/nonpalatal then stopped/continuous g decisions support every B task. The common noninitial-c lexical exception needs the bounded repair PRON-IND-01.
The Fulk rule supports vowel+sonorant environments and the final-ð then f chain in hæfð. hǣlðu/forðām exceptions are honestly supplied; Cook’s different wording is not silently combined with Fulk.
Vowel and consonant duration remain distinct; medial doubling adds no syllable; final doubling is bounded. Unstressed vowels and actual prefix divisions make D/E answerable.
All 25 tasks solved. Meanings, divisions and needed lexical exception are supplied. Reading grammar is not assessed or promoted to recall; its previous solved sound table is absent.
Selected Cook/Fulk conventions and spelling normalizations are disclosed. The source note for the proposed sēcan addition must distinguish its prefixed Fulk witness and Cook variant order.

novelty_and_support.qualification: C6 intentionally reuses the previously supplied hǣlðu reading and the ǣfre comparison. Its prompt explicitly says this is an exception comparison, not deduction; that is bounded guided practice, not a concealed independent test.
novelty_and_support.reused_words: cēosað is reused for initial c and medial/final voice; cwæð for cw and final th. These are different decisions. ǣfre returns in the declared exception comparison.
novelty_and_support.reference_tables: A learner can consult general sound tables, but the tested word/position/combination still determines the choice. Complete references are not treated as leakage.
novelty_and_support.audio_limit: This is a written independent solution and usability/source review, not an audio recording or observation of a learner’s articulation.

Fulk §§20–23 pp14–15/PDF26–27: selected rounded diphthongs, exceptions, prefix/root stress and connected-speech limits.
Fulk §135b p103/PDF115: dīc/dīcas, micel/micles and the prefixed sēcan witness; §135a on the same page supports fæger/regn and the distinct g conditions.

findings.finding: The noninitial-c defaults are carefully qualified, but the otherwise-k/before-back-vowel branch has no named exception. Readers applying it later to the common course verb sēcan could select k, although the infinitive has ch.
findings.requested_repair: Add a compact supplied pronunciation exception for sēcan, seek, beside the noninitial-c comparison. It is lexical support, not a new historical derivation or assessment requirement. Preserve the source variant order in the note and do not imply every form of the verb has ch.
source_evidence: Fulk §135b p103/PDF115 explicitly prints be-sēċan with overpointed c and contrasts stopped sēcst/sēcþ; the be- division makes the root visible. This is a prefixed witness, not a claim that the unprefixed infinitive is the literal printed example.
Cook Vocabulary p311/PDF327 prints sēcan (sēcean) (114), seek; visit.
The current course teaches sēcan in Unit 9, not Unit 2: chapters/ch09/student.md headings at1148/1156 and the secan sense milestone in lexicon/entries.json.
findings.task_impact: No change to any of the 25 actual task answers. Current tasks contain no unsupported sēcan inference.
findings.source_inspection: Fulk p103 and Cook p311 were actually viewed; actual Unit 9 learner headings/register milestone checked.

resolution.text: Learn **sēcan**, “seek”, as a supplied exception: its **c** is **ch** as in *chin*, despite the following **a**. The back-vowel pattern does not override a word's stated pronunciation.
resolution.assessment: The named infinitive supplies the needed lexical exception without teaching history, altering any task, or asserting the same consonant in every inflection. The source note accurately distinguishes the Cook headword variant from Fulk’s explicitly prefixed example.

items.label: A1
items.assessment: Both distinguish brief rounded o from held steady go-type ō; the key refers to the guide’s short-o articulation rather than importing English for/went vowels.

items.label: A2
items.assessment: Both give short bet versus long steady day, deny a separate hook sound, and retain two syllables/final e.

items.label: A3
items.assessment: All three long-vowel values and front tongue/rounded lips for ȳ agree; syllable counts agree.

items.label: A4
items.assessment: All six diphthong qualities, short/long classifications and syllable counts agree. The key avoids an unnecessary syllable-boundary notation used in the frozen answer; see reviewer clarification below.

items.label: B1
items.assessment: Both choose ch from word-initial c immediately before front ēo.

items.label: B2
items.assessment: Both choose ch in micel and k before l in micles, applying immediate-neighbour priority.

items.label: B3
items.assessment: Both exclude the y branch for gān/glæd and then select word-initial stopped g.

items.label: B4
items.assessment: Both choose y in fæger/regn; the key usefully distinguishes g before n from g after n.

items.label: B5
items.assessment: Both select nonpalatal continuous medial g and supply the narrow-gap/voiced-airflow articulation.

items.label: B6
items.assessment: Both give bridge for cg, finger with stopped g for ng, and rounded short y; neither replaces ng with English sing’s final sound.

items.label: B7
items.assessment: Both contrast front h after i and back h after o, preserve breath and t; the key’s extra short-o/two-syllable reminder is consistent.

items.label: B8
items.assessment: Both treat sc as one sh sound despite ū and cw as a joined k+w sequence.

items.label: C1
items.assessment: Both choose voiced v between ǣ and voiced r, explicitly not requiring two vowels.

items.label: C2
items.assessment: Both f letters are unvoiced by word-edge position; no modern-English final v is imported.

items.label: C3
items.assessment: Both select voiced medial s and unvoiced final ð, with separate environments.

items.label: C4
items.assessment: Both reason from unvoiced final ð to adjacent unvoiced f; this is the selected Fulk rule.

items.label: C5
items.assessment: Both choose unvoiced final th independent of thorn/eth spelling; the key properly says this is not permission to respell source text.

items.label: C6
items.assessment: Both preserve supplied unvoiced hǣlðu versus ordinary voiced ǣfre and explicitly bound the exception comparison.

items.label: D1
items.assessment: Both give two syllables, first stress, short i and prolonged tt closure without added vowel/length.

items.label: D2
items.assessment: Both give two syllables, first stress, prolonged nn and audible final e.

items.label: D3
items.assessment: Both give two syllables, stressed writ after unstressed ge-, sounded w+r, and no doubled consonant.

items.label: D4
items.assessment: Both give three syllables, root lǣ stress, independent vowel duration, and no doubled consonant.

items.label: E1
items.assessment: Both select y in supplied ge-, sh for sc, two syllables, root stress and one long ēo glide.

items.label: E2
items.assessment: Both select voiced f between eo and o and exactly three audible syllables.

items.label: E3
items.assessment: Both select voiced th between r and a and explicitly allow a voiced consonant neighbour.
